---
title: "Teaching"
---

I teach research methods and statistics — as instructor of record, as a
graduate teaching assistant for our department's statistics sequence, and
through an annual R workshop series I run for graduate students.

Most of my teaching is with students who arrive convinced they are "not maths
people." The work is usually less about the statistics than about making the
first hour survivable.

## Courses

### As instructor of record

::: {.course}
**HDF 315L — Research Methods in Human Development and Family Sciences**\
[The University of Texas at Austin · Fall 2025]{.meta}

Full responsibility for design, instruction, and assessment. Students carried a
single research idea across the semester, with weekly homework building toward
it rather than sitting apart from it.

## Statistics workshops for graduate students

An annual workshop series for graduate students in Human Development and Family
Sciences at UT Austin, run through the departmental statistics committee. Each
runs in January, before the semester gets heavy.

::: {.course}
**AI-assisted data analysis: Vibe coding with Positron** [· January 2026]{.meta}

Working with an AI assistant inside a real analysis project: what it is good
at, where it silently fails, and the verification habits that make it safe to
use on research code.
:::

::: {.course}
**Data wrangling with R** [· January 2025]{.meta}

Reshaping, merging, and cleaning real messy data — the unglamorous majority of
any analysis, and the part least often taught.
:::

::: {.course}
**Plotting figures with R** [· January 2024]{.meta}

Building publication-quality figures in ggplot2, including the parts that
usually go wrong: legends, facets, fonts, and export settings that survive a
journal's production process.
:::

::: {.course}
**Basic data analysis with R** [· January 2023]{.meta}

A first course for students who had only ever used SPSS: projects, scripts,
reproducibility, and a first pass through descriptives and regression.
:::

In development for the coming year: a workshop on the concepts underneath
AI-assisted research — tokens, context windows, agents, and the command line —
for researchers with no computing background.

::: {.note}
**Materials.** Slides and scripts aren't posted here yet. When they go up they
will be in this site's `files/` folder rather than on a file-sharing service, so
that they load for readers in mainland China. **No workshop datasets will be
posted** — the examples use participant data that isn't mine to distribute, and
I'm rebuilding them on synthetic data first.
:::

## Mentoring

I have supervised undergraduate research projects in the Perry and Benner labs,
and trained graduate and undergraduate assistants in physiological data
collection and preprocessing — RSA acquisition with Mindware, behavioural
coding with Mangold Interact, and the cleaning pipelines that come after.

**What I take from this.** Engagement and course-overall are my weakest numbers
while the instructor-facing items are my strongest, so the thing to rebuild is
the course's activity structure, not the delivery. The contradictory pacing
comments are best explained by the *slides* moving fast while the *course* moved
slowly — so I'm cutting slide density and adding optional depth rather than
splitting the difference. And the request for more elaboration tells me I was
treating a quiet room as an understanding room.

With nine students, low participation is structural rather than a sign of
disengagement, and it needs protocols designed for that size instead of
scaled-down large-class techniques.

**From my TA appointments in the graduate statistics sequence,** the recurring
strengths were depth in R and detailed written feedback. Two things to work on:
one student found my grading somewhat harsh, and I'd rather be exacting *and*
visibly on the student's side; and while several students described the support
as the most useful they'd had, one reported getting little from me all semester.
Availability is not outreach — the students who need help most are the least
likely to ask for it, and waiting for them to arrive is a choice with
predictable results.
